steps.body: Once a shape is split into equal parts, each part gets a fraction name. Split into 4 equal parts, and each one is **one-fourth — 1/4** — of the whole. The bottom number counts the equal parts you cut; the top counts the parts you're talking about. Straight from the fractions course.
steps.narration: Once a shape is split into equal parts, each part gets a fraction name. Split into 4 equal parts, and each one is one fourth of the whole. The bottom number counts the equal parts you cut; the top counts the parts you are talking about. Straight from the fractions course.

widget.prompt: Match each equally-split shape to the fraction naming ONE of its parts.

pairErrors.feedback: Three equal parts makes each one a THIRD (1/3). The bottom number matches the count of parts you cut: 3.

widget.missFeedback: The bottom number = how many equal parts the whole is cut into. One of those parts is 1-over-that-number.
widget.successFeedback: 3 parts → 1/3, 4 parts → 1/4, 6 parts → 1/6. The bottom counts the cuts.

explanationVariants: Eight equal parts means each single part is one-eighth — 1/8 — of the whole.
The bottom counts the equal parts (8), so one part is 1/8.

widget.prompt: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. What fraction is ONE slice?

commonEntries.feedback: 1/1 is the WHOLE pizza — all eight slices. A single slice is just 1/8 of it.
8 is the number of slices, not the fraction for one. One of eight equal parts is 1/8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Eight equal parts means the bottom says 8; one slice puts a 1 on top.
widget.successFeedback: Eight equal parts, so one slice is one-eighth of the pizza.

steps.body: Talking about MORE than one part? Stack them on top. Shade 3 of 4 equal parts and you've got **three-fourths — 3/4**: bottom still counts the total cuts (4), top counts how many you took (3). Same shape-and-count logic as bars and number lines from before.
steps.narration: Talking about more than one part? Stack them on top. Shade 3 of 4 equal parts and you have three fourths: the bottom still counts the total cuts, 4, and the top counts how many you took, 3. The same shape and count logic as bars and number lines from before.

explanationVariants: Five equal parts total (bottom = 5), two of them shaded (top = 2): that's 2/5.
Bottom counts the cuts (5), top counts the shaded shares (2) — 2/5.

widget.prompt: A strip is split into 5 equal parts; 2 of them are shaded. The shaded amount is (top number)/(bottom number). What is the BOTTOM number?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the shaded count — that's the TOP. The bottom counts ALL the equal parts: 5.
3 is the unshaded count. The bottom counts every equal part, shaded or not: 5 in all.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The bottom number counts the total equal parts: how many is the strip split into?

widget.prompt: This shape has 6 equal parts. Tap parts to shade exactly 4/6 of it — tap the 4 parts that make four-sixths.

hotspots.label: part 5
hotspots.feedback: That would make 5 shaded — 5/6. Four-sixths needs exactly four parts tapped.

hotspots.label: part 6
hotspots.feedback: Tapping this makes more than 4 shaded. For 4/6, shade exactly four of the six parts.

widget.missFeedback: 4/6 means 4 of the 6 equal parts shaded — tap exactly four.
widget.successFeedback: Four of the six equal parts shaded = 4/6. Top is what you took (4), bottom is the total parts (6).

predict.prompt: You'll shade 4 of the 6 equal parts. Is 4/6 more than half the shape, or less?
predict.reveal: Half of six parts is three — shading four goes one whole part beyond the halfway mark.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents parts as fractions.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for parts as fractions must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines parts as fractions.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Shading all 4 of 4 equal parts is 4/4 — the whole shape, which equals 1.
When the top equals the bottom, you've got every part: 4/4 = one whole.

widget.prompt: A shape is split into 4 equal parts and ALL 4 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?

options.label: 4/4, all parts shaded
options.feedback: Every part taken: top equals bottom, so 4/4 = one whole shape.

options.label: 0/4, no parts shaded
options.feedback: 0/4 would mean NOTHING shaded. All four parts ARE shaded, so it's 4/4 — the whole thing.

options.label: 1/4, one part shaded
options.feedback: 1/4 is a single part. All FOUR parts shaded is 4/4 — the complete shape.

options.label: 4/1, four parts total
options.feedback: The bottom still counts the 4 equal parts. All four shaded is 4/4, which equals one whole.

hints: First count the total equal panes — that's the bottom number.
The window has 8 equal panes, and 3 are still dirty.
'Cleaned' is the ones NOT dirty — how many of the 8?
explanationVariants: The window has 8 equal panes (bottom = 8). If 3 are dirty, then 8 − 3 = 5 are clean, so 5/8 is washed.
Total parts 8, cleaned parts 5 (the 3 dirty ones taken away): the washed fraction is 5/8.

widget.prompt: A window has 8 equal panes. 3 panes are still dirty; the rest are clean. What fraction of the window is CLEAN?

commonEntries.feedback: 3/8 is the DIRTY fraction. The question asks the CLEAN part: 8 − 3 = 5, so 5/8.
The bottom must count ALL 8 panes, not just some. Clean panes are 5 out of 8: 5/8.
The bottom counts the total panes (8), not the dirty ones. Clean is 5 of 8: 5/8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The bottom counts ALL 8 panes; the top counts the clean ones: 8 − 3 = 5.
widget.successFeedback: 8 panes total, 3 dirty, so 5 clean: 5/8 washed. Bottom counts all panes, top counts the clean ones.

takeaways: Split into n equal parts → each part is 1/n; m parts shaded is m/n.
Bottom counts the total equal parts; top counts the ones you mean.
All parts shaded (n/n) is the whole, equal to 1.
steps.teaser: that completes the shapes trail — and ties every shape back to the fractions you already know.

concept.body: Quick rewind. The fraction name reads straight off the split: **bottom = how many equal parts in all; top = how many you're counting.** Four equal parts, one of them, is 1/4. Two of them, 2/4. Count the cuts for the bottom, count your parts for the top.
concept.narration: Quick rewind. The fraction name reads straight off the split: the bottom says how many equal parts in all; the top says how many you are counting. Four equal parts, one of them, is one fourth. Two of them, two fourths. Count the cuts for the bottom, count your parts for the top.

explanationVariants: The bottom counts the three parts; one of them is 1/3.

widget.prompt: A ribbon is split into 3 equal parts. One part is…

options.feedback: One of three equal parts is one-third.
Flipped — the 3 counts the parts and goes on the bottom. One part is 1/3.
1/1 is the whole ribbon (all three parts). One part alone is 1/3.
